meta.title: Who really said "Existence precedes essence"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Jean-Paul Sartre. His signature formula (l'existence précède l'essence), stated in Being and Nothingness (1943) and the 1945 lecture Existentialism Is a Humanism.
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Sartre. The core existentialist formula, from Being and Nothingness (1943) and Existentialism Is a Humanism (1946) — with Heidegger and Kierkegaard precedents.

answer.sourceLine: This is genuinely Sartre’s signature formula. He states “existence precedes essence” (French ‘l’existence précède l’essence’) in both ‘Being and Nothingness’ (1943) and his 1945 lecture ‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’ (published 1946), where he calls it the first principle of existentialism. The wording is confirmed in the standard English text of that lecture.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Being and Nothingness (1943); Existentialism Is a Humanism (lecture 1945, pub. 1946)
Standard English rendering; confirmed in Philip Mairet’s translation of the 1945 lecture

source.excerpt: Atheistic existentialism… declares with greater consistency that if God does not exist there is at least one being whose existence comes before its essence, a being which exists before it can be defined by any conception of it. That being is man… What do we mean by saying that existence precedes essence? We mean that man first of all exists, encounters himself, surges up in the world — and defines himself afterwards.
trail: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy confirms Sartre uses “existence precedes essence” in both ‘Being and Nothingness’ and ‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’.
The full phrase appears repeatedly in the standard English text of the 1945 lecture.
Wikipedia’s survey notes antecedents in Heidegger and Kierkegaard, but the crisp three-word formula is Sartre’s.

source.rightsNote: The works containing this line — ‘Being and Nothingness’ (1943) and ‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’ (1946) — were first published well after 1931 and remain in copyright in the United States, held by Sartre’s estate and Éditions Gallimard; the English translations (Frechtman 1947, Mairet 1948, and later) carry their own translators’ copyrights. The three-word phrase itself is a short philosophical formula in common scholarly use.

author.metaLine: 1905–1980 · French philosopher, playwright & founder-figure of existentialism
author.bio: Jean-Paul Sartre was the central figure of 20th-century French existentialism, author of the philosophical treatise Being and Nothingness (1943) and the play No Exit. His formula that human beings first exist and only afterward define themselves — “existence precedes essence” — became the movement’s defining slogan. He declined the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature.

misattribution.heading: Correctly Sartre — but the story has two twists
misattribution.intro: Unlike most quote-magnet lines, this one really is Sartre’s. The common errors are about where it comes from and who invented the idea, not whether he said it.

items.who: “It’s a direct quote from Being and Nothingness”
items.why: Sartre does affirm the formula in ‘Being and Nothingness’ (1943), but the clean, oft-quoted three-word slogan is delivered most explicitly in his 1945 lecture ‘Existentialism Is a Humanism’, per the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy.
The wording is his, but the thought has clear precedents: Heidegger wrote that “the essence of Dasein lies in its existence,” and commentators trace antecedents to Kierkegaard and Schelling.

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: the phrase is authentically Sartre’s — his own formulation, stated in his own works — even though the underlying idea has philosophical ancestors.

context.heading: Why the line mattered
lead: Sartre’s claim inverts a long tradition. For most of Western philosophy, a thing’s essence — its defining nature or purpose — came first, as a blueprint precedes the object. Sartre says that for human beings the reverse holds: we exist first, without a fixed nature, and only afterward define ourselves through our choices.
The consequence he draws is radical freedom: with no God and no given human nature to fall back on, “man is condemned to be free,” wholly responsible for what he makes of himself.
context.pull: “Man first of all exists… and defines himself afterwards.”
